NEA J HOP
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Lawrence Brown
by Patricia Willard
Reel One

Los Angeles, California
July 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

P R O C E E D I N G S
June 12, 1976. Interview with Lawrence Brown.

Well now, let's start with correcting your birth date. I think you said you were looking at the Feather John Chilton's Who's Who of Jazz and Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia of Jazz, and which one is the right one?
Well, there have been several errors from time to time. I guess I gave out the wrong information from time to time, but my real birth date is August the 3rd, 1907. That's in the Chilton book.
Okay. So that's the date (inaudible).
Yes.
And you were born in -- where?

I was born in Lawrence, Kansas, and my father was a minister. So therefore we were moved any time the Conference moved us, and I spent only a short time in the whole Kansas area. I would up to about my sixth year. And from there we were moved to Oakland, California, and from then on I've been in the western area.
Were you named for the city you were born in?
No, I think I was named after Paul Lawrence Dunbar. I think I heard my mother say something about knowing him or something of Paul Lawrence Dunbar.*
What denomination was your father?
He was an A.M.E. minister. He'd also been a presiding elder. He'd been in the church practically
all his life.
And are you -- what are your earliest recollections of music?

I think my mother played for the choir way back in Kansas. I have a faint recollection of her playing organ. That was when you used to pump the organ by foot, and we were in a town called Fort Scott, Kansas, and that was my first recollection. From then on the rest of the time that I was in Kansas, I was just -- I did nothing in music, because I was too young. In fact, I left Kansas when I was about six or seven. So I had no interest in music at all.
Did you sing in a choir?
No.
No singing?
No singing.
(Laughter)
How large was your family?
Three boys. [PAUSE]
What was your father's name?
J. M. Brown, John M. Brown.
What was your mother's name?
Maggie Brown, Maggie Mae, I think it was.
And your brothers?
Oh, Harold Brown and Merrill Brown. 2 musician.
I know Harold is in the business.
Yes.
How about Merrill?

Oh, he's dead now. He was a very, very good piano accompanist and concert type player. And he was in Oakland, around the Bay area, and we had a fairly large church up in that area, and all of the concert singers that used to give concerts at the church, they would request that my brother accompany them. He was very good at that.
So both Harold and Merrill played piano, right?
Right, uh-huh.
And what instrument did you start on?

I really started on tuba. Possibly an explanation of why I started on the various instruments is because in Oakland, California, they had a very good school system, and if your parent would sign a bond, you could take out any instrument that you wanted to learn. And so I took out tuba, and I stayed with that for a while until I became fairly well acquainted with the three-valved instruments, and -- in fact, I got so good on the three-valves, that I could play a solo. And one of my first solos was 'Silent Night,' which I played at the Christmas festival in our church.
[PAUSE]
That was when you were about what age?
Oh, I was about nine or ten years old then, uh-huh.
And how long did you play that instrument?

Well, it got too heavy for me, and for a while I didn't know which instrument to pick up then. And I finally acquired a taste for violin, and I liked it so well that I used to try to make violins out of cigar boxes with boards and everything. And I had some very good friends in the church, and one old lady decided to give me a violin for Christmas, much to my chagrin. As it turned out, I took it for a few months, oh, quite a little time. In fact, I would say almost two years or more, during which -- [PAUSE]

Now, as I said before, my father being a minister, we were continually shifting around and different things, and the choir leader of our church was a trombone player, and he used to use his trombone only on Sunday, and so it stayed up in the vestibule of the church. And I keep -- kept noticing this horn laying there, and, now, being interested in music, I wondered what kind of sound this was. And I finally got nerve enough up to open it and try to make a note.

Now, since I had been playing tuba, the lip positions are very similar, and so I could make a note or a few notes, and the orchestra leader of our orchestra in school was a pretty good teacher at most any instrument, and so I applied to him for some lessons, which he granted, and so he taught me my first lessons on playing the trombone.
Well, the trombone at that time was more or less a tailgate instrument, you know, that the slur and -- a tailgate type of thing. And --
Did that interest you at that time?

--the -- no, I wasn't interested in tailgate. I by this time had had enough music and enough acquaintance with most all of the instruments, and I happened to remember that the trombone was about the same tonal level as the cello, and the cello was the violin, just a large violin in the lower registers. So the trombone, having nothing but a slide, I thought of the trombone as the violin of brass instruments, and then I began to wonder why couldn't the trombone play the same type of music as the cello, and I couldn't see why it had to still resort to that tailgate business.

So I began to try to play melodies, using the melodic type of playing instead of the tailgate type, which I enjoyed quite a bit. I liked to play melodies, and I'd had enough all-around, we'll say,music, so I would practice airs and different songs, different things like that on the trombone, and still it seemed that nobody was doing this very much, at least out on the coast.
Do you remember about how old you were when you were trying these things on the trombone?
It was around 12, I think it was, because, as I said before, shifting so much and acquiring so

much music, I couldn't -- I didn't keep track of dates too well. I just knew that I wasn't -- I was in grammar school into high school, and by this time I had gotten so I could play in the grammar school orchestra on trombone and the high school orches- tras on trombone, and of course my father was a very, very strict person, and it was all right for me to play melodies and church pieces and in the choir, finally, on trombone, but no jazz or no dance -- whatever you call the dance type music at that -- in that era.
Did you think that was what you wanted to play?

Well, I wanted to play all of them. Our family had a feeling, it seemed, for music, and we could acquire a capability of playing any type of music. I tried everything from symphony to concert to jazz, all those music. It seemed very easy for me to acquire the feeling, and so by the time I was into high school, I was playing all of these different types of music fairly well. Of course, I was continually in the school bands, the school orchestras, and I had even gotten so I could play in the school dance band, which used to give per- formances at noon hour. During the noon hour we'd go up in the gym, and they would have school dances during the noon hour.
Now, by this time I'm over in San Francisco, and I remember one of the associates in our dance orchestra very well. His name was -- his name was Phil Lambert, and later -- many

years later I ran into Phil Lambert, and he was the director of the pit orchestra at the Fox Theater in Washington, D. C., and he told me he was going from there into New York into some orchestra, but I never saw him any more. But by this time I was thoroughly interested, and trombone was my instrument.

From this time on began my very intensive study of trombone and of the music that I would like to play on it. As I said before, I could never get the idea out of my head that if a cello, who was a sort of a slide instrument also, or a violin, could play melodies, why couldn't a trombone, which was a slide type instrument. They couldn't play melodies instead of the usual oompah or whatever, dixie type playing that was done on it. And so, therefore, I would rehearse for hours and hours, playing melodies, listening to tone and trying to improve my conception of how I wanted the instrument to sound. I would sit up after school and way up in the night with no lights on and just listen to the tones come back from the walls and phrase things as I would like to hear them, until I became quite adept at the playing of these melodies, plus the regular score type trombone in school orchestras, and by now music was my primary interest.

It wasn't very long, or within the span of the next year or so, that my family was again moved, and this time we were moved to Pasadena, where I entered Pasadena J. C. I was in the orchestra there and by this time was playing well
enough. I played in the shows, in the school plays, in the shows and school concerts and for soloists accompanying soloists and different people and --
Can you remember what year it was in Pasadena?

Now, that was around '23, 1923, and at -- as I said before, at that time there were a great number of musicians, because we had no TV, and we had very little radio, because I remember when we were a couple of years younger, we used to build our own crystal sets. That was the only thing we had in radio. A radio set was very, very expensive, far too precious for my pocketbook or our pocketbook. And so we had a lot of musicians, a lot of good natural talent that was used.
To go back a bit to San Francisco, I believe you were telling me earlier that you and your brother had played together. Which brother was that?
Oh, the younger brother. The older brother was eight years older than I was, so we --
Older brother was Harold?
No, Merrill.
The oldest one.
He was a piano -- concert piano type. And in fact he used to accompany me whenever I wanted to play a solo in church or something like that.
So you and Harold played.
We played together quite a little bit.
And that was with which instrument.

I was trombone; by this time he had taken piano, and he was very good on piano. It seemed odd, but we were all very adept at understanding the styles and different feelings that we wanted to get out of our instruments. So we worked together quite well. In fact, later on we even played in the same orchestra.
All three of you or --
No, just two of us.
-- you and Harold?
The other one stayed in --
I know you mentioned your mother played organ. Did your father play any instrument?

No, he used to -- he could play a little piano, and he was the singer. He came from a family of singers. He had one brother that was quite famous in a quartet that traveled all over the world back then, and his brother's name was James Bartlett Brown. I forget the name of the quartet. Oh, they were on the Orpheum circuit or Pantages circuit for years, and he traveled all over. In fact, the whole family was very musical.
I read in one of the biographical sketches that at Pasadena College you were studying pre-med.
Yes, I later became interested in
medicine, but it didn't supercede music. It was a second -- my second liking, preference -- or my preference.
Was it your intention at that time possibly to become a doctor, or was it just you were studying because you were interested in the subject?

I was interested in the subject, and there was a faint desire that maybe someday I would like to become a doctor, and I took this along through school, the physiologies, the chemistries and different things like that, and the thing that sort of discouraged me was when I made a trip to a hospital -- the class went to the hospital -- and seeing the different things in the hospital and the people and sick and different things like that, I soon realized that I could never operate. Also we must remember that in those days there wasn't much specializing to the extent that it is now in medicine, and therefore you had to be more or less a general practitioner. And so I just put the idea of medicine out of my mind, because I was quite sure that I could -- if I'd lose one patient, I'd be through with medicine anyway, so -- forget it.
At what point in your study of music did you decide that you wanted to become a professional musician?
I -- well, that became almost a necessity. That was more or less later on. As I said before,
my father being very, very strict and me being very interested in music, I used to pull some capers that didn't fit with his way of thinking at all.
What kind of capers?
Well, we used to wait until he went to bed, and then we'd slip out the side window, and I'd go downtown and listen to the dance bands and things. In those days it was very safe. And --
Do you remember what bands you heard in that period?

I used to go all the way over to Los Angeles to hear the Sunnyland Band, which was very popular. And, oh, several -- any band that came through the lower California area, there used to be quite a few of them that would come through, and so I'd slip out and go.
Do you remember specifically any band that you saw?

I think I heard King Oliver one time. And mostly the general -- just the local bands, which, as I say, in those days the bands in person were quite good, many of them quite good, and invariably the next day somebody would come back and tell my father, 'I saw your son last night.' He said, 'I don't see how that can be possible. They were home in bed.' And so that continued and continued for quite a time.
Now, when you and Harold would do that,
you had -- from Pasadena to Los Angeles is how far, about ten miles, 12 miles?
Well, in fact I did it alone. I didn't take Harold. Harold wasn't that interested. And we used to catch the red car -- called the red car down ON Fair Oaks -- and ride over.
You'd take the great big street car.

Yes, big red car. And the dance let out at 1:00 o'clock. So therefore we'd have to leave a little early so we'd catch that last red car going back to Pasadena and slip back in the window and get in bed so no one was the wiser, until it just kept up so long, that my father got suspicious and --
You got caught?

No, never got caught. Different things just kept up, and I kept slipping out, going to different places, and that's when he would suspicion and question me. And then we would have a set-to, and finally at the age of 18 he just put it to me bluntly, 'If you continue to do this, you'll have to leave my house.' So I told him, 'I think I will,' which he like to have fainted, but I didn't leave Pasadena. I stayed in Pasadena.
But you left home then at 18.
But moved out of the house. So that he said I was disgracing him by going out in this jazz business.

He couldn't stand that in any form. So I moved out to my cousin's house up in North Pasadena, and I was still going -- trying to go to school, which I did for a while, but finally had to quit, and from then on I was a professional musician.

I think I was out of work for about two weeks, when a friend of mine who I'd known through school up in Oakland, by the name of Charlie Eckels, had an orchestra that worked over here in Los Angeles in a place called 401 Ballroom, which was one of the establishments where they usually call these places dime-a-dance parlors.
And that was in Los Angeles?
Yeah, on North Main Street, yes.
401 was the address?
Yes, 401 North Main.
And that was in 19- what?
I would say that was about '40 -- I mean '27, the early part of '27, very early.
And you were telling me earlier about how much money you made there.
Oh, we made the phenomenal salary of $40.00 a week.
And that was high for that time.
That was nice. That was good. There was no tax. There was nothing, you know, to be taken out. It was just plain -- you didn't even have an income tax or anything.
And how many nights a week did you play?
Six nights a week. Six nights -- these things are hard to remember, because musicians in those days changed places so often, that you didn't keep track of too many of the things like that.
How many -- how big a band was it?
We had five or six pieces, six pieces, I think, and a couple of the fellows are still alive from that orchestra.
Who are they?
One of them is named Bill Griffin.
And what did he play?

He played saxophone. And the other -- I don't remember the other names. Oh, one of them was the drummer, was named Baby Lewis. I think he's down in Texas somewhere. And I don't remember too many of the other names.
I think you mentioned that it was somewhere around then that you joined the Musician's Union, wasn't it?

'27, yes, I joined the Musician's Union in the latter part of 1927, and it was very new at that time. In fact, our union office was in the garage of one of the fellows, back in the alley there off of Central Avenue.
And was the -- in those days there were
the two locals --
The two locals, yes.
(the black local and the white local --(inaudible) the 767 and 47.
The 47, yes, I'm pretty sure it was.
And was the one that was in the (47) garage.
Right. Right, uh-huh. And later they moved to a house on Central Avenue.
Do you know what year that 767 was formed (inaudible)?
No, I don't. It was before me, because they didn't have a house, or they didn't have an office. We all went in this fellow's garage and paid our dues and things like that.
How much were you paying?
I don't even remember that. It was very little. I know that.
Was the union really active then? Did it go around and check and see whether places were hiring union members?

No. No. It didn't do much work such as union work then. It was just getting started, and they were just trying to cultivate a membership more than enforce the laws and bylaws. I think 47 was fairly well situated, but they just looked on 767 as, oh, well, they're over there, and
they get what they can or what's left over and -- So at that point in those days there weren't many benefits from being --

Oh, no, no, you just paid your dues, and you didn't get anything out of it. At this point I would like to inject one of my favorite recollections. It happened when I was over in Pasadena College. Lionel Hampton and Les Hite came west from Chicago, and one of their first stops was to play a school dance over in Pasadena.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Lawrence Brown
by Patricia Willard
Reel Two

Los Angeles, California
July 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
At this point I'd like to inject one of my favorite recollections. There were two fellows that came out West from Chicago. One was named Les Hite, the other was named Lionel Hampton.
And their first job in California was a little dance date at Pasadena College which I was lucky enough to play with them at. And that was my first meeting with the great Lionel Hampton.

Of course at that time he was a drummer. And his only other musical activity was the two finger playing on the piano which a lot of you remember or even have heard records of -- which he was most adept at.
Well at that time was -- just the two of them came out and hired Los Angeles musicians to play with them for their concert, or what?
Now I think there was a piano player -- we had good musicians over there too. I think Henry Prince, a very good piano player, was one of the members of the group.
There were only five of us at this dance engagement so -- it's so far back you know. That's years and years, and centuries ago. So I don't remember too much about it.
But I distinctly remember because later on, I became very close with both of these fellows.
Uh-huh. Do you remember who all played
No. Piano, drums, saxophone, and trombone. And I think that's the only instruments. I don't think there's any -- it was a small -- one of these small school dances you know. A little class things.
Well that would have been about 1921.
Around '25 or '6 -- long in there. I don't remember exactly.
Were either Les Hite or Lionel Hampton well known in this area?
No, no, they were just coming out I think on their own. I don't know why they came even. But they came out and I was one of the first that met them.

One of the things I wanted to ask you -- going back a bit -- is when you talked about your sudden intensive study of the trombone, starting when you were in San Francisco. And you talked about all of the things that you did personally, experimenting with sound and sounds. Did you ever at any time on the trombone have private instruction, or was all of your formal instruction in school?

Yeah, it was -- most of it was in school until I got into Los Angeles where I was more or less in the professional life. Of course in Pasadena we had some pretty good instructors. In those days there were very, very good instructors in the school system.
They were usually members of the symphonies, or some musical aggregations -- very prominent in the cities. But they were good. It wasn't just a case of people that didn't know what they were doing.
I remember one instructor was assistant director of a symphony in San Francisco, and things like that. They were good men.
And that person taught in the public schools.
Yes, they were in the city school system because schools didn't pay too much -- or like they do now. And it helped you know -- enhance all of their salaries.
Would you remember that individual's name?

One of them was Alfred Nord. He was a violin man in Oakland. And the woman in San Francisco -- had a woman teacher -- a woman head of the orchestra -- Miss [crossed out: Ma.] Neppert. She was an older woman.
Do you remember how to spell the name?

N-e-p-e-r-t, I think, Miss Nepert. And then the teacher in the Pasadena was a Mr. Parker. And an interesting feature there was that his wife played cello and she used to come and sit in with the class quite often and play along with us.
In fact, we became so close that when I would go out
and do solos, like at the different churches, and you know -- things like that -- she would accompany me. She was also a piano player.
She would go along and accompany me.
She probably had a very good feeling for your approach to the trombone.
Yes.
With your feeling about the cello.
Yes.
Which of those teachers that you mentioned was the one associated with the symphony? You said is it the one in San Francisco -- is that right? Or in Oakland.
In Oakland. His name was Alfred Nord.
Okay. What was it -- was there on Oakland Symphony then? I know there is now.
Now that I don't remember. I don't remember whether he came from Oakland or San Francisco. Of course it's just across the Bay.
Uh-huh. Another question I had -- when you left your father's house and moved in with your cousin, was your cousin involved in music in any way?
No. He was a landscaper. But he was you know -- very lenient. He was a nice old fellow.
Sympathetic.
Yes.
your cousin's name?
What was his (inaudible)?
Isn't that something --
Well, maybe it'll come to you later on.

And when you used to go into town in Los Angeles and Pasadena to listen to the bands, were there other musicians that you played with in the school bands that would go too? You said we at one point. I wondered if there were any other musicians you took with you or --
No, that is one of my deep afflictions. When I mean I, I say we. I don't know whether that's a coverup from the old days or what. But I keep using the plurals instead of the singular.
Eckols
leader
And Eckols, your first professional (inaudible) -- what did Eckols play --
Eckols

Trumpet. He was a trumpet player, yeah. He was a trumpet player. The cousin I was speaking of was Oscar Over. He used to be a judge up here in the central part of California in one of the little courts up there somewhere.
And he had retired and became a landscape gardener.
What about Harold -- when you left home because of your music, did Harold pursue music, or was Harold that interested in jazz?
No, Harold was in school about three years or so behind me so he was definitely in school then, but he later on became first interested in pipe organ. And he took

from one of our organists in the church, a Professor Keaton, who was in Oakland. And finally -- I don't remember just how the situation culminated, but he finally sought of went in professionally too. And he went his way and I went my way.

Of course we weren't living together then anyway. So the family went our different ways -- all in music, except the older one who was by this time well in the Post Office -- Postal Service in Oakland.
I read in Barry Ulanov's Duke Ellington book that your first spectacular musical appearance was before a Mother's Day crowd of 6,000 at Aimee Semple Mc Pherson's Temple in Los Angeles.
Yes.
How old were you then?

Well, I had to be around 19 or close to 20. Of course that's a little later on. No, that was in the latter part of the school era, because there was a club -- a men's club over in Pasadena. And they brought me over to the temple as a soloist with their club meeting.
There were -- Miss Mc Pherson had a radio station upstairs. And they came over to do a stint in the station. And they brought me along. And I played a number on the air at her temple.
And as luck would have it, she came up there during the program, and I was playing, and she seemed to have never

heard anything played quite like that. And so she personally invited me to come down and play at the Mother's Day program, much to my -- well whatever you want to call it -- because I never saw that many people in my life.
And needless to say I was perfectly petrified. I didn't know which end of the horn to blow. But some way we got through it and that was the beginning of my really, really great musical career.
Do you remember what you played for the Mother's Day crowd?

I played Schubert's 'Serenade' -- I think that was the name of it. The thing that had the least notes in it. 'Cause I never saw 6,000 people in front of me, a hundred and some people behind me in the choir, a hundred and some people sitting on the side of me in the orchestra, and that infernal red light on that broadcasting machine. That was a little too much.
A funny thing. In all my musical career, I never forgot that -- that feeling of complete mystification of all of this thing going on at once. And until today I'm terrifically stage frighted --
Really?
I never -- I never got over that fright, no, that's a funny thing.
When you played on the radio for the
first time, before the Mother's Day occasion, do you remember what you played on your first radio appearance?

I think it was the old tune called ["Infamadus."](PHONETIC). And of course I had no fright then. I just tried to blow the tubes off the air. But, when I saw these people, the fright struck me and I've never gotten over it.
Well it never shows.
Oh yes, yeah, it showed inside. Yeah, I never could -- I was never at ease, and I've never been satisfied with anything I played since.
Because of not feeling at ease?
Yeah.
How about when there isn't an audience?
Oh, I can do anything I want when nobody's there. But the minute you see that -- those people out there, then something happens.
How about in recording? When there's only your fellow musicians and no real audience.

It's all right. Everything is all right then until I have to solo, and immediately the feeling of insecurity sets in. And I begin to become a little confused as to what I want to play, and how I want one thing to follow another.
You always come through sounding so
serene, it's hard to believe.

Well, I don't know how to explain that. In fact, recording I've always been a little confused anyway because in my efforts, tonal wise, I've always tried to emphasize the open tone -- the "oo" sound. And in recording, the "e" sound is very important. It cuts through so that it relaxes that monotonous oo-ness on records.
Uh-huh. So are you satisfied -- or are you saying you're not satisfied with your recordings?

Well, I'm not satisfied. I've never been satisfied. That is probably why that until today, I have very, very -- in fact, I never even collected a record. I would -- I didn't want any. I didn't want to hear that again. So I don't --
So you don't have your own records?
I don't have any records. Since I've been out of music, I've had several of them given to me. But they're home on the shelf. I don't play them. I don't even have a record player.
That's too bad.
No, I don't --
One other question -- do you remember who the musician was whose garage 767 was in?
His name was Robinson. He was primarily an automotive mechanic. And he was an older fellow. And as
I said, they didn't have money enough to hire a hall or have a place of their own, so this old man was just good enough to allow them to use the back room of his garage.
Did he play an instrument with your group?
I don't remember whether he played anything or not.
I, I wasn't necessarily a part of the union --
He was -- I think he was secretary. He worked -- not worked, but he acted as secretary. I think Mr. Robinson was secretary. I was too young at the game to pay any attention to that side of it.
How did you happen to join the union?
Well, it became imperative. The union was getting power. And you joined the union, you're way ahead you know. You're eventually going to do it anyway, so you might as well be ahead.
So that was -- you joined in the end of 1927 and it was in the beginning of 1927 when you started working professionally at the 401.

Right. And I'm glad I did because 30 years later I had my -- I received my gold card from the union, which means you've been in the union 30 years. And the benefits from then -- you pay no more dues and the benefits came later
on for being in the union.
Uh-huh. What was your next job after the 401? That was pretty steady there for awhile, right?

Yes, it was steady. I think it lasted the latter part of '27. Then I begin to hop around. I went to another dance hall called Danceland, which was down the street, and around August or so, I was invited to join a band called The Quality Serenaders.

It was a band that at that time was working out of the Cotton Club which was the biggest night club in the West. And oneof their members was sick and he had to move back to Chicago. And he happened to be a trombone player.
Taylor was his name. And so I took his place. And that was the beginning of the big time cabaret sessions.
And they had where -- a steady house band there.

But that was my forte at that time. I'd get many calls over come play me so and so. And I would play this in this sub-tonish fashion. You must have been getting a following right about that time.
Yeah, I had quite a little following. Of course the money was short. But it was something that I was quite proud of -- to be able to do.
Was Curtis Moseby a musician or just -- I know he owned a club and -- did he lead a band?
He was originally the drummer. In fact, he drummed several times when he'd come over -- you know -- come up and play a few sets and things like that.

But Duke wouldn't have had the 13 --
Oh, he's very superstitious. Very superstitious.
Do you remember any of his other superstitions?
Don't put any buttons on the piano keys, was one. Like if you had a button -- take a button off your
shirt or your coat, or something like that, don't put it on the piano keys. He wouldn't sit down there.
(Laughter.)
And let's see, I don't know what else. I can't -- I didn't stick that close with anyone.
I remember, never give anyone a present for their feet, socks or shoes or slippers.
Oh, yeah?
Because it means they're going to walk away from you.
Where did all these things come about?
Well, John Levy told me that's an old theatrical superstition. The first time I ever heard it was from Duke when a friend of his gave him a pair of slippers.
Yeah.
And he got very upset. He said, "Take them back, take them back. That means that you want me to walk away from you."
Well, the only thing I ever heard was the fish and chips in the dressing room, in England. And the peanuts, something about peanuts.
I don't know about those one.
I don't have any superstitions. I haven't got sense enough.
What was the superstition about fish and
You don't eat that in the dressing room in England. Bad luck, something. So --
I know -- (inaudible.)
I never take any cognizance with these things, because I don't believe in anything like that.

I know that he would put up his congratulatory messages and telegrams on opening night, and they couldn't be taken down, and they were to be left there when he left the premises; when he left the engagement, he'd leave them because it was bad luck to take them down.
My only superstition was I never got enough money.
(Laughter.)
Well, that's hardly a superstition.

This is June 19th, 1976, and this is Reel Four of the interview with Lawrence Brown. Lawrence, I noticed in a couple of books references to the alto saxophone at least -- that you played the alto saxophone very briefly, and when you were very young. How long did you play the alto? How old were you?

Oh, I don't exactly remember how old, but I guess at that time I was more or less just jumping around, trying to find some sort of an instrument that I would like. And it was an attractive horn in that they made them -- finished them with all kinds of colors in those days. And that probably attracted me first of all. And then I wanted to get a better acquaintance with reed instruments. I didn't know. There was a possibility that I might like reed instruments. So, I picked it up and tried it for a while.
You said that saxophones were made in different colors.
Yes, red, green, blue, any color you wanted, similar to the way they finish off pots and pans now with that porcelain stuff.
But the basic instrument was brass?
Oh, yes. Yes. The base -- of this -- all of this was just a covering over the basic brass instrument.
Do you remember what color saxophone attracted you?
No, I had no special color. I was just interested in the tone. In fact, at first the -- C- melody was the popular instrument. I don't think alto had gained too much recognition in those days.
But it was the alto that you played, right?
No, I forget which one. I think it was the C-melody. Because I don't remember when the alto first came into prominence.
When you played the saxophone, was this after you played the tuba and before you played the violin, and where in the progression?
It was after the tuba all right, but I don't remember exactly. I was fumbling around with almost any instrument to try to get the sound in my head and find out whether I even liked it or not.
About how long did you play the saxophone?
Oh, I think I put that down in about a couple of months. It had too many keys on it, and besides that reed had a peculiar feeling, and I didn't care too much for that.
Back to the brass mouthpiece.
Yes, I prefered them a little better.
You mentioned that when you were with Curtis Mosby at the Apex in Los Angeles, that you would sometimes go to San Francisco to play a show.
Yes.
Whereabouts in San Francisco did you play with Mosby?

Well, Mosby set up two clubs, one in San Francisco, and one in Los Angeles. And this club in San Francisco was kind of on the second and third floor in a building -- it was right at the beginning of Chinatown. I more or less think it was on Bush and between -- let me see. What were those streets up in there. Between Grant and Kearney. Right there. I think it was Bush Street. It was a north and south street it was on.
But it was up on a second and third floor right down in town, and it was very popular because it was a new type of thing. And its situation down town among all the hotels, why it did quite well.
And that club they called the Apex also?
The Apex, yes. San Francisco Apex.
We've sort of jumped back and forth from the Apex to the Cotton Club but -- so I'm not quite certain how long you were with Curtis Mosby. How long did you

Well, it was a few months. I don't remember too much because between the times at Curtis' place, we would do many some dances, and then we'd go down to Los Angeles and go back in the Cotton Club, and in and out and around like that. It's kind of hard to remember back as far as 1928, and '29.
But you played at the Cotton Club until you went with Mosby, and then you left Mosby to go back to the Cotton Club, is that right?

Right, they changed bands, and as I said before, Lionel Hampton and I had contracts with the Cotton Club, not with the bands that came there. We -- we went in and out, and most of the time stayed regardless of who came.
And when you first went into the Cotton Club you said that you were replacing a trombone player who had left and that his name was Taylor. I didn't get his first name.

I think it was Lewis Taylor. He was a boy from Chicago, and I think he was sick and he had to leave the west coast and go back to Chicago. And that gave me a chance to join that band. At that time it was called the Quality Serenaders, Uh-huh.
When we were talking about studying the trombone, and I asked you if you had ever studied
privately, you said not before you went to Pasadena. Were there any private lessons on the trombone in Pasadena?

Just a few here and there. There was Doc Hyder a few times, and this one and that one. I tried to pick up because I felt that I could -- I only wanted the mechanical structure from teachers. The tone and all of that I would like to create myself, so --
Doc Hyder -- was he a full time instructor, or was he a professional musician?
Oh, yes. He had a -- he had a teaching -- he taught out among the trees. Kind of outside. And he was a very good teacher. But I didn't spend any time with anyone. I was too busy working.
Was he in Los Angeles or Pasadena?
In Los Angeles. Kind of in between the two -- you know, Pasadena area.
I see. Then the next part of the private instruction you had was in New York, is that right?

While I was in the theaters and things in New York, we'd contact or run into these different good teachers. I would say -- come on and teach me a few things, your secrets and all. There was several of those kind of fellows, and one was a saxophone teacher of all things. He -- but he was very good. He had a terrific ear for getting the tone and the different attack. His name was Caruso. I
can't think of his last name. He just had a reunion here not long ago and invited us all back to -- to his reunion in New York, but I was unable to go because I was in Washington at the time.
Caruso was his first name or his last name?
No, that was his last name. He was a well-known saxophone player among the smaller bands around New York.
And you studied trombone with him?

Yes, I took a few lessons with him. Mostly on breathing and things like that, you know. And then there was Larry -- Larry -- oh, I forget his last name too. He was a terrific breathing man. He taught using the diaphragm to accentuate the notes, punch the notes and give power to the notes.
Was he in New York?

Yeah, he was in New York then, but he's out here now. He's sort of half way retired. Oh, yes. I meant to mention. My friend that I was speaking of was named Larry Collins. Collins is his last name. And his teaching and his playing was especially attractive to me because he used to play such things on trombone as the "Flight of the Bumblebee" and things like that. He'd walk into a radio station cold, we'd call, you know, with no rehearsal or anything.
And he had such beautiful control. And he'd go in to play the "Bumblebee" right off.
That was in New York?
Yes, New York.
Were the teachers that you studied with surprised with your ambition at achieving the tone and the tone that you had achieved at that point? Had they ever heard anybody else --
Well --
(who was striving in the direction you were on the trombone?

-- no, because I never did much playing for them. I usually listened to them and tried to practice the little studies that they gave me to practice. So, they never heard me play. And I did my own work studying by myself for the different methods that I wanted to use for playing.
Was there any standard method that you studied?

Well, usually everyone used the old Arban method. That was the standard book, and if you could play anything in the Arban, you -- you could really play. See so, that was the standard study book going around.
You also mentioned that at one point you and your brother Harold worked in the same orchestra. Which
Yes, that was Les Hite's band in Los Angeles out of the Cotton Club. I didn't work very long with him. Just for a short time.
You were there quite a while --
Oh, I was there but he wasn't no. He's -- he usually plays by himself. He doesn't play with orchestra at all.
He still -- does he still --
He still -- oh yeah, he's still playing.
Solo piano and --
He's solo pianist out at the Beverly Wilshire in the [Bedrina] Room. So, he's worked practically all his life by himself that way.
He has quite a following in Los Angeles.
Oh --
You mentioned that your first recordings were around 1930. Who were the first ones with? Was it Paul Howard or Louis Armstrong?

Well, the first recordings I would say were around '29 because Louis didn't come here until '30. And it was around '29 and we were -- I was in this band called Quality Serenaders. And we had a contract with Victor. We made about -- what was it -- six, or eight, or ten records
with Victor. That was the first time I had recorded.
And all of those were with Quality Serenaders?
Yes, that was the only band I played with or made any records with besides Louis Lewis out here.
I found a reference in a book to "Charlie's Idea": A series of variations on the chords of "Tiger Rag". Was that one of the ones you made with the Quality Serenaders?

Yes. Yes. That was one of them. Now, this Charlie was incidentally Charlie Lawrence, and Charlie Lawrence was one of the men in the band that when I was in school, I used to slip over from Pasadena to come over here and here. And I was playing with Charlie Lawrence in this band of the Quality Serenaders?
Was he a member of the Sunnyland Band you mentioned?
Yes, the Sunnyland Band -- they used to come over here.
Who else was in that band? Do you remember?

Oh, let's see. There was James Porter. He was a very good trumpet player. Very strong. You could hear him down about ten blocks. And, oh, let's see. Who else? William France was the tenor man, and Ashford Hardy was

the trombone. And his name is pretty big down in this area. And a fellow by the name of Wilson was on piano, but I can't remember his first name. But they had a real fine band. They were very popular.
How big a band was the Sunnyland Band?
It was about -- let me see -- eight or nine pieces. Eight or nine pieces. But they played like 15 or 20.

On your recordings with Louis Armstrong you mentioned "I'm in the market for you", "Ding Dong Daddy", "Confessin'" and "Confession". And then I found a reference to "If I could be with you". Was that at the same time as the ones that you mentioned?
Yes. Yes. That was one of the same bunch that we made.

Getting back to your first days or weeks with Duke, the first date you played with Duke you said was at the Colonial Theater at Hartford, Connecticut where you played "Trees", and your first recording was the "Shiek of Araby" in New York. How much space of time was there between your first live appearance in the band and the first recording session?
Well, let's see. In those days we were playing these theaters week after week all the time. It was theaters one after another, and in between would be these

dance dates. And I don't remember too well how much time it was, but I know we were always doing something. And recording of this number "Shiek of Araby" was done in New York, I remember that much. And it wasn't too long after I had joined the band.
Do you think weeks, or months, or a couple of months, or --

Well, I'd have to look up in discography to find out the exact, you know, time between the numbers. Because as I said, we were always doing something. If it wasn't rehearsing, and we did a lot of club dates in which we carried a show -- a little floor show -- and we'd have to reherse for that. It's hard to remember any certain period.
Well, you -- you joined Duke out here in February, was that right?
Well, it was the week after Easter, I remember that, in 1932.
Oh, and -- well, according to the discography by Ashland, "Shiek of Araby" was recorded in May -- May 16, 1932.
Could be, yes. Could be.
It must have been recorded almost immediately.
Well, not too long. Of course, there was a little period I had to lay off.
Getting across country, you mentioned.
Yes.

The reason I asked was that some musicians I know play for several months before they even get a solo in dances or concerts and -- or club dates with Duke, and for you to just record right away a solo was unusual at least in terms of the later band. I don't know whether it was --
Oh.
-- that unusual in the band at that time.

No, I came into the band as a soloist. When Irving Mills heard me in California -- the Cotton Club -- I was doing a solo in the show. And this particular night, as I think I told you, was when Donald Novis, one of the fine singers of that period -- he went got to Pasadena the same time I did. And so, I played this "Trees" in the show at the Cotton Club. And he asked Don to sing the chorus, or take a chorus of it. And he did. So, therefore we were playing together this same number.

But even though other musicians were soloists before they joined Duke, they did not always solo immediately with Duke, and so the fact that you did I thought might be unusual. I think it was in terms of the later day band. But --
Well, they sort of considered me a new addition to something. I don't know.
You were very special (inaudible).
No, it was just a new addition, a new funny sound. So, I was soloing from the beginning almost.

At the time you joined Duke, the 12 members of the band were Johnny Hodges, Barney Bigard, Harry Carney, Arthur Whetsel, Cootie Williams, Freddie Jenkins, Joe Nanton, Fred Guy, Wellman Braud, Sonny Greer, and Duke, is that right?
Right. Uh-huh.
And you and Tizol and Tricky Sam became the first three-trombone section, is that true?
I believe so. One of the first. There weren't too many bands that had three as yet.

One of the books I was reading said that this was the first three-trombone section at that time, but the book's aren't always right, I know. You said that when you first joined, your salary was $70.00 a week providing that the band worked seven days.
Right.
And you said that in one band you joined, everybody was making $125.00 a week. Was that the salary in Duke's band at the time you joined?
Yeah, that was the basic salary.

Everybody made the same thing except me. Well, of course, Hardwicke when he came. He didn't make $125.00 either. I don't know exactly what he made, but $70.00 was my salary. And if you worked two days, you got two-sevenths, and if you worked all week you got it all, but --
When you first joined the band, were they working every day of the week, or do you remember?

Mostly. Mostly every day. The only gripe I had really then was the fact they had no restriction on the number of shows. Now, I was playing this solo sometimes five and six times a day, plus all of the band music -- first chair in the band, and it was kind of hard. I couldn't see that. I never could see that from the first.
Five and six times a day would be what? Theater or --
Theaters. Yes. Theaters.
(Interruption in recording)
Do you remember how long you stayed at that salary?

I think it was almost two years. As I say, I don't have all of my records, pay slips and stuff, but for a while I used to keep every one of them. And then they got misplaced when I'd like leave one house, or one home and cut out. And so now I hardly have any. But I have some books that statements are in. But that was the way it was. And you paid everything except your transportation. So, I distinctly remember one time when we left New York to go out

on a New Year's Day or a New Year's performance, and I think we stayed out there almost two or three months with no work. And we just layed around the town. And the next date was past there, so we didn't come back to New York. We were living -- all of us living in New York then.
Well, you said that when you joined the band you had some savings, so --
Well, they --
-- you survived that, but what about people who might not have had any savings. What did they do?

I don't know. I don't know. But you see, for instance, if you had -- I know I had about $7-800.00. And a meal -- you could go down to the restaurant and get a very good meal for 35¢ in those days. So, it lasted quite a little while. The rooms were a dollar, two dollars a night.

In Barry Ulanov's book on Duke Ellington, there is a statement that says on the "Shiek of Arabia", Lawrence plays what he says was one of the only two solos that he ever planned through from beginning to end. The other one was "Rose of the Rio Grande". Is that true?

Partially. Partially. The only thing is that whenever I would be given a solo, you know, where the whole number sort of depended on me, I would plan the whole number. I had a system which I used to try to perfect these solos. I wouldn't get up and just play anything that

came across my mind. I would first go into a study without the horn. I would mentally play the lead -- I mean the theme, then with slight deviations, and then with more deviations, and then hear where the band would come in and make embellishments, and then I would come in with more.
And when I got through with this routine, I could hear myself play the number as I wanted to hear it, and still not have touched the horn. Then after that, I'd pick up the horn and play it.
So that you did that everytime, not just on the two that -- the two instances.

No. No. No. I did that almost every time. You see, in that band also, when you were given a solo that nobody -- that's your composition, your composition for that particular -- the way you wanted to hear it played. I mean you routine it the way you want it. Nobody framed it for you. Said play this, play that. No, you did that yourself. And it usually worked so that it would sound the best to yourself, see.

At a recording session, you'd have to do that pretty rapidly, wouldn't you, because the recording session that -- some that you've mentioned and some I've been at, Duke would sometimes pass out the music, and then you'd play it.
Well, most of the time the music at

recording session had been played several times at dances and theaters and things before. Then you finally thought it was good enough to record. Then you'd go in and record it. After you've played it a number of times, you pretty well had what you wanted to play set in your mind. So, therefore, it didn't take too long to work it out.
But several times that extemporaneous playing came about. I distinctly remember one or two numbers that I did that on.
Do you know what numbers they were?
One number was this tune called "Blue Light".
That's the one that later became --
That became "Translucency", and my theme from "Blue Light" was what they used to make the whole number of "Translucency".
And that was one that you had not planned. That was --

That was one that I wrote that number when he pointed to me and said take it. Take a chorus. And from somewhere, I don't know, that melody just came to me as a relief from the -- what the notes and things that had been going on with the rest of the band. The other part of the number sounded very "mood indigoish", and no particular melody. So, when I came -- when it came to my part, a melody just
Do you remember another occasions when what number it was when -- (inaudible) --
Oh --
-- you did it on the spot?

Well, not too much on the spot, but most of the others I had planned. And another thing, in playing a tune I always kept the idea that there should always be some semblance of the melody, and never get too far away so they couldn't can -- so that the public couldn't tell what you were playing. And so, although you may play around the melody for a while, but come back to it so that they could identify it and say oh that's so and so.
Uh-huh.
And because if you did -- if you played around on every tune, what tune would it be, see. The melody has to come through enough so you can identify one tune from another.
Uh-huh.
And I used that system all the time.
Was there a great deal of musical cooperation among the members of the band when you first joined it, or was there rivalry or competitiveness?
No, they were just like a bunch of brothers. Everybody looked out for each other and helped each
other.
A good -- a good spirit then?
Yeah, very good. Very good.
Did that include Duke too, or did Duke hold himself apart as he did later?

Well, at first he was very much together with the boys. He had learned to what they were doing. But later on when he got confidence in himself -- and he didn't need them anymore. So, he went by himself. Also the management encouraged him to go with them and by himself because in that way he would leave the idea in the public's mind that he was the almighty.
The star syndrome.
Right.
At the time you joined the band, they had their own railroad car for traveling, didn't they?

They had a very good setup that way. They had a manager by the name of Sam Flashnik, and, of course, Irving Mills was the impresario. And we would have, if it was a daytime trip, we would have a private coach, a parlor car usually they would call them. And our car would be attached either to the very front of the car section, or the very back. So that the general public didn't go through our car very much. Now, at night we would have two sleeping cars, a dining car, and a baggage car. That was our section of the train.
You had your own dining car too?

Yes, most of the time. Most of the time except in emergencies. And I've seen this manager, Sam Flashnick [Flizshnik], stop the whole train and wouldn't let it move until they put our car in the proper position. He was very good. One of the best managers I've ever seen. The road manager.
How long was he the manager?
Oh, I would say about ten years or so. I think then he got kind of sick or weak or something.

I've read that when you did have your chartered cars on the train that when you reached your destination, your cars would be parked off on a siding in the city where you were appearing, and that would be your accomodations in that city, is that correct?

Yes, that was right. Providing the stay there wasn't going to be too long. Only in certain sections of the country did we live on the cars for as long as a week at a time, but like for a couple of nights or something like that, they would just park them on the siding. And it would just depend on the conditions of the town. Sometimes we wouldn't even have to use the dining car because they had nice dining rooms in the station, or whatever, you know, was like that. But usually very nice that way.
How long did that private railroad car arrangement go on?

Well, we didn't keep it all the time, only as I say -- they would get the order the Ellington party is leaving such and such a station, such and such a time, requiring two sleepers, and a dining car and a baggage car. See, it would be too much trouble to move that baggage everytime you turned around because we you had huge sets on the stage and stuff. And so they would keep that -- Sonny Greer's setup alone.
(inaudible).
Oh, yeah. A lot of times. Sometimes they would let all the rest of our cars and things go and keep the baggage car on the siding. So, whatever was the most convenient for the outfit.
When you compare the -- those accommodations you had with your own section of the train with later years riding the band bus, which accomodations were more comfortable?
Oh, there's no competition.
That's what I thought.

The band bus was something else, although we had some of the best buses they had. But that uneasiness of being on the highway was much different than having a nice, comfortable berth. And you see, when we were on the train, our berths -- we didn't have to make them up. They didn't have to be made up until we got into the town. So, we could lay there and look out the window, or do whatever they wanted
to do. Sometimes the boys would play cards all day. And it was sort of a nice arrangement they had.

Of course, you also probably had less hectic schedules in those days when you had to depend -- yet they were dictated by train schedules rather than in later years where you took a plane had to play, and then you took the bus and --
Oh well, I don't know how I would say that. It just depended on when we had to get to the next job and -- that we would take -- how long we would keep these cars and things.
From your description of your own sleeper and your own dining car, it sounds a far cry from what I saw when I rode the bus.
Oh, yes. Yes.
In 1958 when you -- it was Howard Johnsons in the middle of the night, if it was a Howard Johnsons --
Right.
-- and the bus was what? Hot in the back and cold in the front.
Oh, you know for many years we had buses that didn't even have a restroom on them.
Yeah, well there was --
-- and they'd have to pick their stops and everything like that. Very bad.
I can remember the bus from here to San Francisco -- I believe it was in 1950 with the band -- and there was trouble finding a restroom that would accomodate the band in a small town.
Right.
And that was probably a problem, wasn't it?
Quite often. Quite often. Would you believe it? One time I rode a bus all the way from Seattle, Washington to New York City.
Mm.
Yeah, straight through.
That's -- that's the band bus?

Yeah. Yeah. We had a driver that could stay up looked like forever. And, of course, I wouldn't do it now because the danger wasn't as -- I wasn't conscious of the danger like I am now. But the -- imagine a man sitting at the wheel 12, 15 hours.
Bad as Harry Carney (unintelligible), huh?
Yeah, he used to like to do that too.
He used to play, when I was on the road with the band we would play a date and then get on the bus, and the band would sleep on the bus --
Yes.
-- until maybe noon the next day.

We'd get to the next destination and then get out, check into a hotel, and maybe get to sleep, (but) probably not. You'd just change your clothes and go to the job. Harry Carney would have been driving all that time, and then he'd go play.
Yes.
He must have been (inaudible). never slept,
Well, he was just crazy about driving. Some people love to drive, and he was just crazy about doing that sort of thing.
Never saw him yawn on the stand either.
I don't know. I was too busy. Yeah.
You said it depended on what part of the country you were in whether or not you stayed on the train on the siding. Was it generally in the South that you stayed on the -- on the train?

Well, mostly I would say because there were more homes or more hotels and places to stay up in the Northern. And usually when -- the first time we ever went South was in '34, and, of course, we didn't know anything -- anyone down there. And naturally it was easier and cheaper for us to stay on the train than get out and try to find places.
So, in '34 you did stay on the train the whole time?
'34 -- for several years when we made
trips that way where we'd stay mostly on the trains. Were there colored hotels in the South?

I don't know that I would recommend them at that particular time. There were some, but not what -- I wouldn't call them hotels even. Certainly wouldn't want to stay there. And the best thing I thought -- or the best thing we did was hit the job and get on out. Leave. Because accommodations were very poor except in people's homes. There were some beautiful homes.
Was it ever difficult to find private accommodations in homes?

What would happen is that when shows or bands or things were coming in town, they had a sort of a committee that would have the rooms listed -- people that wanted to rent their rooms. And when we got to town usually the agent or whoever it was came down to the train and assigned us to the room to go to, and we went to people's -- different people's homes and stayed that way.
It was a regular network sort of a system --
Yes, and --
-- all through the Southern cities.
The next -- the next band that came down, they would do the same thing for them. So, it usually became known that Mrs. so and so has two rooms over there.

Mrs. so and so has three rooms, you know, like that. So, they got along fairly well. And it got so it was real nice because we also usually would eat at the place we stayed. And that was real great because -- some beautiful cooks.
To you knowledge, was there any other band that had its own railroad car like Duke's did?
I don't remember right now. I don't know. I couldn't say.
I've never heard of any other band having one but I --
Yeah. Oh, Cab -- he did the same thing. And there were a few, but just a handful.

Again, in Barry Ulanov's book, he mentioned that John Hammond wrote about you saying after he first heard you with Duke, "He's a virtuoso of the first rank, one who is very conscious of his technical ability. Probably no other trombonist has his equipment, but I'm afraid that this brilliant musician is out of place in Duke's band." And then there's some quotes from Spike Hughes (of The Melody Maker) who felt that you were too sophisticated for jazz and Duke Ellington. Do you remember that?

Well, I -- I can see what they would mean because the era before me -- well, colored bands didn't play sophisticated music. They were jazz bands. You know, the old tail gate type or roughous type of music. Very few of them

played real sweet. And since that was my type of music, why that's all I knew. In fact, that's all I was going to play because I -- for the first years when I was out on the road, I had California in my eye, and I was going back at the drop of a hat. In fact, I left my car on blocks the whole time I was on the road for about 20 years and -- because I didn't care anything about the road, you know. I would go home in a minutes. So, I can see where they thought that was (unintelligible).
